actions.evaluations:
**A2UI** — This is the only candidate whose architecture makes the agent a first-class author of the interface rather than a feature bolted onto it. Three layers: Core (protocol), Agent (skill generation, validation), Renderer. You register your components in a JSON Schema catalog; the Agent SDK's skill generator derives the model's instructions from that catalog, so the model can only emit components and properties you registered; the renderer maps the resulting adjacency-list component tree onto host widgets. The protocol carries data bindings as JSON Pointers (`@path`, absolute vs. relative scope, list templates), agent-side and renderer-side functions, `requiresUserActivation` gating (a function like `openUrl` MUST fire only inside a user gesture — a passive binding is rejected with `EXPRESSION_ERROR`), and catalog composition constraints (`allowedParents`/`allowedChildren`, surfaced as `UNALLOWED_PARENT`/`UNALLOWED_CHILD`). Crucially for the "across web and native" requirement, the site lists official renderers for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose, and the Android side is genuinely published: `androidx.a2ui.compose:compose-runtime|compose-ui:1.0.0-alpha02` and `androidx.compose.material3:material3-a2ui:1.0.0-alpha02` are live on Google Maven — i.e. the Material 3 implementation of the A2UI Basic Catalog ships as an AndroidX artifact. The honest trade-offs: A2UI is a protocol plus SDKs, not a visual language, and its own roadmap states "Today a custom component still needs an implementation on each native platform," with described primitives, a runtime templating engine, and a secure sandbox for shared business logic still planned; the Dart Agent SDK lacks skill generation; the published Android artifacts are alpha, not 1.0; and the repo carries 481 open issues. What addresses the objection: the v1.0 spec deliberately decouples branding so the Basic Catalog "takes its styling from the host framework's theme" — meaning you keep Material 3 on Compose, SwiftUI controls on iOS, and your own tokens on web, and A2UI is the contract that lets a single agent target all three. ([repo](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui), [spec v1.0](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/), [roadmap](https://a2ui.org/roadmap/), [overview](https://a2ui.org/), [Compose artifacts](https://dl.google.com/dl/android/maven2/androidx/a2ui/compose/group-index.xml))

**json-render** — The runner-up, and a genuinely more complete *framework* than A2UI in some ways: a flat `{root, elements}` spec, Zod catalogs, `catalog.prompt()` to build the system prompt, a richer expression layer (`$state`, `$cond`, `$template`, `$computed`, `$bindState`), `watch`/`setState`, devtools, an MCP server, and a renderer matrix that runs from React/Vue/Svelte/Solid through React Native, Next, TanStack Start, Remotion, React PDF, React Email, Slack/Teams chat, Ink terminal, images and Three.js. Its React Native package ships real components (Container, Row, Column, ScrollContainer, SafeArea, Pressable, TextInput, Switch, Checkbox, Slider, SearchBar, Spinner, ProgressBar, Card, ListItem, Modal…) with a `defineCatalog`/`defineRegistry` split that constrains agent output exactly the way A2UI does. What stops it winning is the native axis: its only native renderer is React Native — there is no SwiftUI or Jetpack Compose renderer — so iOS-native and Android-native products are out of scope, and it supplies no visual language of its own (its components are shadcn/RN primitives). Objection addressed: if my native surface is React Native and I want a working generative UI in a week rather than a spec-conformance program, json-render is the faster pick, and its lower open-issue count (123 vs A2UI's 481) argues for it. I passed because "across web and native" is a hard requirement here. ([repo](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render), [React Native package](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md))

**MCP Apps** — The best distribution channel for agent UIs and the one I'd pair with A2UI rather than choose against it: `ui://` resources, `text/html;profile=mcp-app`, mandatory iframe sandboxing with host-declared CSP for connect/resource/frame/baseUri domains, explicit permission requests, and working hosts including Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose and Postman. The architectural problem is the payload: it is HTML in a sandbox, so it cannot produce native widgets and it lives outside your design system and your a11y tree — A2UI's own generative-UI spectrum makes this exact contrast, noting that code-generation/HTML delivery is "tied to web & WebViews" and "ships heavier HTML/JS payloads rather than native mobile or desktop widgets." Objection addressed: A2UI supports rendering a surface inside an MCP App and embedding MCP Apps inside an A2UI surface (`McpApp` shares data paths with sibling components), so MCP Apps is the transport, A2UI is the contract. ([repo](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps), [SEP-1865 spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx))

**CopilotKit** — The strongest agent runtime, but a framework, not a design system: six generative-UI primitives (Components as Tools, Tool Call Rendering, State Rendering, Reasoning, A2UI in Dynamic and Fixed Schema flavors, and MCP Apps in sandboxed iframes), AG-UI co-authorship, bidirectional shared state through `AGUISendStateSnapshot`/`AGUISendStateDelta` over SSE with a reactive `useAgent()` hook, WebMCP, and Channels for Slack Block Kit and Teams Adaptive Cards. Its significance for this decision is that it already ships A2UI support — which is why I treat it as an integration partner rather than a rival, and why I read its adoption as evidence (my inference, not a claim in the docs) that A2UI is becoming the common denominator. Objection addressed: if you pick CopilotKit, you still need a UI contract underneath it, and that contract is A2UI. ([repo](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [generative UI](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/concepts/generative-ui-overview), [shared state](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state))

**Vercel UI SDK** — The sharpest implementation of "agents and people use the same screen" I found: `createAgent()` installs a bridge that lets an agent `snapshot()` the page's components (ref, label, value, available actions), `query()` list items by text, and `act()` to change values, with permission callbacks, `details.source === "agent"` hooks, and `registerTools` exposing those three tools to a browser's built-in agent through `document.modelContext.registerTool`, annotated `readOnlyHint`/`untrustedContentHint`. But it is a behavior library, not a design system, it is explicitly in beta (created late October 2026, 53 open issues), and it has no native renderer — React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components only, no React Native, Swift or Compose. Objection addressed: for a web-only product I would pick UI SDK over A2UI, because it lets a running agent manipulate live controls rather than only emit screens; the brief's native requirement is precisely what disqualified it. ([repo](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui), [Connect an Agent](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent), [WebMCP](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/webmcp))

The problem is maturity, not vision: the repo was created 10 October 2026, shows 0 stars and 0 forks with 116 open issues, its Apple half "has not reached a first stable version," and Android and Windows are "open for a builder." Objection addressed: it is worth watching — and because it already speaks A2UI, adopting it would not lock me out of the protocol — but I would not put a production native surface on a month-old, zero-adoption repository with no stable package to pin against.
